data:
Packtrix v0.1.0 is the first release. It builds signed APT repositories for Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 and Debian 12 and 13; RPM, vendor repositories and bundles are planned, and each page marks what isn’t implemented yet. The manifest API is v1alpha1: names, fields and commands may still change in later releases.
Start with Getting started, then the Overview, Concepts, the Manifest reference and the Workflow. Architecture and Security are for contributors and for anyone reviewing the trust model.
Getting startedBuild offline repositories for Ubuntu and Debian, serve them, and install from them, step by step OverviewWhy Packtrix exists, who it is for, what it is not, and how it relates to other tools ConceptsTargets, packages, repositories, dependency resolution, baseline, lockfile, snapshots, bundles Manifest referenceEvery manifest field, its default, and the validation rules WorkflowThe commands, the connected and offline sides, updates and approvals ArchitectureHow resolution, download, metadata generation and publishing work SecurityHow trust flows from upstream vendors to your machines, and how HTTPS and GPG are handled Built-in catalogWhich distros and vendor repositories are built in, and how Packtrix picks them RoadmapDelivery phases and decisions that are still open ReleasingHow releases are cut, and how to verify one before installing it
Status: partly implemented. For contributors and reviewers. The APT pipeline, from expand to publish, works as described; RPM, bundles, and the parts marked planned don’t exist yet.
data.a-repository-not-an-installation#A repos:
apt and dnf choose exactly one consistent set of packages to install on one machine. Packtrix builds a repository that machines install from later, with their own apt or dnf. The repository must contain everything a machine could need, and the machine makes the final choice. So Packtrix computes a dependency closure, not a single solution:
Start with the listed packages. A version constraint such as 1.34.* selects an exact version. For each dependency of each package in the set, skip it if the baseline or the set already satisfies it. Otherwise add a provider: the first alternative of a | b (every alternative with alternatives: all), a real package before a virtual one, and the newest version that satisfies the constraint. When a package breaks or conflicts with the baseline version of another package, add the newer version that the machine’s apt or dnf will upgrade to. Repeat until nothing is added. An extra package costs a little space; a missing one makes an installation fail offline. Where the two could differ, Packtrix includes rather than omits.
The resolver’s output is a list of (name, version, architecture, source repository), which the lockfile records.
data.baselines-from-metadata#Baselines from m:
The baseline is computed from the target’s own metadata, at the versions of the distro’s release, not its latest updates:
minimal, APT: Essential packages and those with Priority: required or important, plus their dependencies, which is what the distro’s installer puts on a minimal system. They come from the release suite’s main component, such as noble/main. minimal, RPM: the @core group from the repositories’ comps.xml. none: nothing. lock:: the package list of a discovered host, at its exact versions. Release versions matter for machines installed from older media: if a package needs a newer libssl3 than the release shipped, that update is included.
data.building-repository-metadata#Building re:
Packtrix publishes a subset of upstream repositories. Instead of regenerating metadata by reading every package file, it copies the matching entries from the upstream metadata:
APT: the stanzas for the selected packages are copied verbatim from upstream Packages files; only Filename changes, to pool//…, so two upstream repositories can’t collide. Packtrix writes Packages, Packages.gz and Packages.xz with their by-hash copies, and a Release with Acquire-By-Hash: yes, SHA-256 sums and no Valid-Until, signed as InRelease and Release.gpg. Its Date is the newest of the upstream Release files, so the same lock always gives the same metadata, apart from the signatures. Package files are hard-linked from the pool, or copied across file systems. The stanzas come from the upstream indexes as plan saw them: plan caches each verified Release under the digest the lock records, and its indexes under their SHA-256. Without the cache, Packtrix fetches the Release again, and refuses it if it changed since: “run packtrix plan”. RPM: the entries for the selected packages are copied from upstream primary, filelists and other metadata (plus updateinfo and modules where present), and Packtrix writes a new repomd.xml. This keeps upstream fields intact, is deterministic, and doesn’t depend on apt-ftparchive or createrepo_c being installed. createrepo_c is only needed for packages that don’t come from an upstream repository (a planned feature).
For each target, the distro packages and the vendor packages are merged into one repository, so every machine needs a single source entry.
data.bundles#Bundles:
(Planned.) A bundle is a tar.zst archive containing:
the snapshot’s metadata and the package files it needs (a delta bundle contains only the files the receiver doesn’t have yet); the lockfile; a signed bundle manifest listing every file and its SHA-256. import verifies the bundle signature and every file hash, writes into the pool, and publishes the snapshot the same atomic way.
data.checking-against-apt-and-dnf#Checking ag:
The resolver must agree with the tools the machines run:
Nightly, in CI: for every built-in distro, in clean containers (test/e2e): Packtrix publishes test manifests, and the real apt installs every listed package from them; sets of packages (a small server, alternatives and virtual packages, Kubernetes node prerequisites) are resolved by Packtrix and by apt itself, from the same repositories. The check fails if apt picks a package, or a version, that Packtrix’s closure doesn’t contain, and reports what the closure has beyond apt. It also runs on pull requests that change how packages are read or resolved. (Planned) The same for dnf. (Planned) Optionally, on your side: packtrix sync --verify-install runs the validation step when podman or docker is available. Containers are used for these checks only. Producing repositories never needs them.
data.code-layout#Code layout:
Implemented:
cmd/packtrix/ binary entry point internal/catalog/ built-in distros: repositories, components, keys pinned by fingerprint internal/build/ the published repositories, one signed repository per target, and the machines' client files internal/cli/ commands (cobra) internal/version/ build information internal/deb/ Debian versions and how they sort, dependency fields, Packages indexes, version constraints internal/download/ the lock's packages into the pool, checked against the lock internal/expand/ manifest + catalog → each target's repositories and packages internal/fetch/ HTTP downloads: proxies, private CAs, credentials, retries, resuming internal/pgp/ signature verification against pinned keys, signing internal/plan/ plan: read the repositories, resolve each target, what to download and why internal/publish/ sync: download, build a snapshot, switch current to it internal/pool/ files stored by SHA-256: the package pool, the index cache internal/resolve/ dependency closure, independent of the package format internal/repo/apt/ reading upstream APT repositories, verified; writing the published ones internal/repo/apt/apttest/ signed APT archives served over HTTP(S), for tests internal/resolve/apt/ APT dependency model internal/secret/ secret references: env:NAME, file:/path pkg/apis/packtrix/ internal API of manifests and locks, used by the rest of Packtrix pkg/apis/packtrix/v1alpha1/ format v1alpha1 of manifests and locks: types, defaults, generated conversions pkg/apis/packtrix/scheme/ registers every API version pkg/apis/packtrix/validation/ validation of the internal API pkg/apis/packtrix/manifest/ reading and writing manifests and locks test/e2e/ publish, then install in clean containers of each distro The API follows the Kubernetes pattern, with two kinds: OfflineRepository, the manifest, and Lock, the lock that plan writes. A file is decoded in its own version, defaulted with that version’s defaults, converted to the internal API, then validated. A future version adds a package next to v1alpha1/ and registers it in the scheme; the rest of Packtrix doesn’t change. The deepcopy, defaulting and conversion code (zz_generated.*.go) is generated by make update-codegen.
Planned:
internal/catalog/ vendor repositories, auto-detection internal/resolve/ RPM dependency model, baselines internal/repo/rpm/ RPM metadata subsetting and signing internal/lock/ lockfile diff internal/publish/ garbage collection of the pool, rollback internal/bundle/ export and import internal/validate/ optional install tests against candidate snapshots, in containers
data.fetching-and-the-package-pool#Fetching a: Every package file is checked against the SHA-256 in the upstream index, and that index is checked against the upstream signature (see Security). Files are stored once, by hash: pool/sha256/ab/abcdef…, read-only. Snapshots and targets reference the pool. The same kubelet.deb from the Kubernetes repository is stored once even when three Debian-family targets use it. A download goes to pool/partial/ first. It only moves into the pool once its size and SHA-256 match, so an interrupted or corrupted download never appears there. The partial file keeps its name across runs, so the next run resumes it; one that doesn’t match is deleted, and the next run starts over. Downloads are resumable and cached across runs. A sync after a small upstream change downloads only the changed files. Upstream indexes are cached the same way, by the SHA-256 that the signed Release file gives, in $XDG_CACHE_HOME/packtrix/indexes (usually ~/.cache/packtrix, or --cache-dir). The Release file is always fetched, since it says what is current; an index the cache holds isn’t. Cached files are checked against their hash each time they are read, and indexes that no run used for 30 days are removed.
data.pipeline#Pipeline: manifest ──► expand ──► resolve ──► lock ──► fetch ──► build ──► publish ──► export │ │ │ │ │ built-in dependency verify subset atomic catalog closure in Go, upstream upstream switch of from upstream signatures metadata, `current` metadata + SHA-256 sign Stage Input Output expand Manifest and built-in catalog Every target with concrete repository URLs, components and pinned keys resolve Expanded targets, package list and upstream metadata For each target and architecture: every package the machines need beyond the baseline lock Resolution result packtrix.lock fetch Lockfile Package files in the content-addressed pool, each verified build Pool and lockfile Repository metadata for each target, signed validate (optional, planned) Candidate snapshot Proof that apt/dnf install every listed package from it publish Built snapshot current switched to the new snapshot export (planned) Snapshot (and optionally an earlier lockfile) A full or delta bundle
data.publication#Publication: /srv/repos/ ├── current -> snapshots/2026-10-22T020000Z ├── snapshots/ │ ├── 2026-10-15T020000Z/ │ └── 2026-10-22T020000Z/ │ ├── apt/ubuntu-24.04/dists/noble/… apt/ubuntu-24.04/pool/… │ ├── rpm/rocky-9/repodata/… …/Packages/… │ ├── keys/ │ ├── clients/ │ └── packtrix.lock └── pool/sha256/… A snapshot is fully built in a hidden directory before anything points at it. A sync that fails or is interrupted leaves current and the published snapshots as they were. current switches with a single atomic rename of a symlink, so clients never see a mix of old and new. Package files in snapshots are hard links into the pool, so a snapshot costs only its metadata. publish.keepSnapshots earlier snapshots are kept next to the current one. A lock file stops two sync runs from writing the same publish path at once. (Planned) APT repositories set Acquire-By-Hash: yes, and earlier metadata files stay reachable for a grace period. A client that fetched the old InRelease just before the switch can still download the matching Packages file. (Planned) Garbage collection removes pool files that no kept snapshot references.
data.requirements#Requirements: Side Needs Connected The packtrix binary and outbound access to the upstream repositories (directly or through a proxy). podman or docker only for --verify-install. Offline The packtrix binary (for import); any static web server to serve the files
data.resolution#Resolution: Packtrix resolves dependencies itself, in Go, from the metadata of each target’s repositories: Packages files for APT, primary.xml and filelists.xml for RPM. It needs no container runtime and no apt or dnf binary, so a Rocky target resolves on an Ubuntu machine and the other way round.
data.the-engine-and-the-models#The engine and:
The closure loop, in internal/resolve, knows no package format. It runs once per target and architecture, on packages that are exact versions, and asks a model for two things: what a package needs, and whether the baseline has a package. The APT and RPM models translate their formats into needs:
A need lists groups of candidates. The model orders each group by preference: a real package before a virtual one, the newest version first. If any candidate is already in the set or the baseline, the need is satisfied. Otherwise the engine adds the first candidate of the first non-empty group, or of every group with alternatives: all. A need can have a condition: a list of packages. It only applies once the set or the baseline contains one of them, even if that happens later in the loop. A need without any candidate is a failure. The engine collects every failure with its path from the listed package, and records why each package is in the set, such as libfoo1 ← nginx ← listed. Dependency Need APT Depends: a (>= 1) | b One group for a: its versions from 1 on, then the packages that provide a. Then one group for b APT Breaks: libfoo (<< 2.0) Condition: the versions of libfoo before 2.0. Candidate: the newest libfoo RPM Requires: libcrypto.so.3()(64bit) One group: the packages that provide the capability RPM Requires: /usr/bin/python3 One group: the packages whose file list contains the path RPM (a or b) Two groups, as for APT’s a | b RPM (a and b) Two needs RPM (x if y) Condition: the packages that provide y. Candidates: those that provide x RPM (x unless y) x, without a condition: the engine has no negative condition, so it includes rather than omits So the RPM model plugs in without changing the engine.
data.validation#Validation:
(Planned.) With packtrix sync --verify-install, Packtrix starts a clean container of each target distro before publishing, points it only at the candidate snapshot, and installs every listed package with apt or dnf. If any install fails, the snapshot isn’t published.
This step is optional, and it is the only one that needs podman or docker. The same install tests always run in Packtrix’s own CI.
data.what-the-resolver-handles#What the resol: APT RPM Depends and Pre-Depends, alternatives (a | b), versions compared with dpkg’s rules Requires on capabilities and Provides, versions compared with RPM’s rules, including epochs Virtual packages through Provides File dependencies, such as /usr/bin/python3, through filelists.xml Breaks and Conflicts against baseline versions Boolean dependencies: (a or b), (x if y) Multi-Arch and Architecture: all Modular content on EL8: packages of streams that aren’t enabled are hidden, as dnf hides them Recommends, when resolve.recommends is on Weak dependencies, when resolve.recommends is on; Obsoletes

data:
Status: partly implemented. The built-in distros today are ubuntu-22.04, ubuntu-24.04, debian-12 and debian-13: packtrix catalog list shows them. The other distros and the vendor repositories below are planned.
The catalog is Packtrix’s built-in knowledge of repositories: URLs, components, architectures and pinned signing keys. It lets a manifest say distro: rocky-9 instead of listing URLs and key files, and lets Packtrix find vendor repositories on its own.
data.auto-detection#Auto-detection:
You list packages, not vendor repositories. For each target, Packtrix decides where each package comes from:
for each package in the manifest: 1. available in the distro (or in your extraRepos)? → use it; the distro always wins 2. otherwise, look it up in the catalog for this distro and architecture: no repository provides it → error, with "did you mean" suggestions exactly one repository → add that repository a versioned family (kubernetes) → choose by the package's `version`; no version → error several unrelated repositories → error: ambiguous, set `repo:` then add any repository the chosen ones require (epel → crb) and resolve dependencies. Rules that keep this predictable:
Rule Why The distro always wins nginx exists in Ubuntu and on nginx.org. Silently swapping in a third-party build would change what you run. Opt in per package with repo: nginx-org. Versioned repositories need a version Picking a Kubernetes minor version silently could break version-skew rules. version: "1.34.*" selects kubernetes@1.34. Only top-level packages trigger detection Dependencies must resolve from the repositories already chosen. Vendor packages depend on their own repository or the distro, so this covers real cases. Everything is visible plan lists each repository that was added automatically and which package caused it, and flags new signing keys. The lockfile records the source of every package. Organizations can refuse autoRepos.deny: [epel-*] blocks a repository. autoRepos.enabled: false turns detection off completely. Only built-in distros Targets defined from scratch with repos have no catalog mapping, so detection is off for them.
data.built-in-distros#Built-in distros:
Used with targets[].distro:
Family Names Notes Ubuntu ubuntu-22.04, ubuntu-24.04, ubuntu-26.04 amd64 comes from archive.ubuntu.com and security.ubuntu.com; arm64 from ports.ubuntu.com. The catalog handles the difference. Debian debian-12, debian-13 Rocky Linux rocky-8, rocky-9, rocky-10 AlmaLinux almalinux-8, almalinux-9, almalinux-10 CentOS Stream centos-stream-9, centos-stream-10 CentOS Linux 7 and 8 are end-of-life and not included RHEL rhel-8, rhel-9, rhel-10 Requires distro.auth with your subscription certificates Every distro entry defines its official repositories (for Ubuntu: release, -updates, -security), default components and signing keys.
data.built-in-vendor-repositories#Built-in ve:
Added automatically when a listed package needs them (see auto-detection):
Name Provides deb rpm Notes docker docker-ce, containerd.io, plugins ✅ ✅ kubernetes@ kubelet, kubeadm, kubectl, cri-tools, kubernetes-cni ✅ ✅ One repository per Kubernetes minor version; chosen by the package version cri-o@ cri-o ✅ ✅ One repository per minor version nvidia-container-toolkit nvidia-container-toolkit and its libraries ✅ ✅ epel- Extra packages for Enterprise Linux — ✅ Community repository. Turns on crb automatically, which EPEL requires. Later, based on demand: helm, hashicorp, postgresql, grafana, nginx-org.
Container tools such as podman, buildah and skopeo are already in the distro repositories and need no vendor repository.
data.catalog-entry-format#Catalog entry forma:
The catalog lives in internal/catalog/ and is embedded in the binary: catalog.yaml holds its version, distros/.yaml one distro each, and keys/.asc the keys. A distro entry looks like this:
# internal/catalog/distros/ubuntu-24.04.yaml (excerpt) name: ubuntu-24.04 family: ubuntu # ubuntu, debian or el format: apt release: { version: "24.04", codename: noble } architectures: [amd64, arm64] components: - { name: main, default: true } - { name: universe, default: true } - { name: restricted } repositories: - name: security url: https://security.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ archURLs: # where an architecture lives elsewhere arm64: https://ports.ubuntu.com/ubuntu-ports/ suite: noble-security keys: [ubuntu-archive-2018] # → keys/ubuntu-archive-2018.asc baseline: { repository: release, component: main } keys: ubuntu-archive-2018: F6EC B376 2474 EDA9 D21B 7022 8719 20D1 991B C93C RPM entries have no suite. Their URLs contain {component} and {arch}, and a component’s path gives its name in the URL, such as PowerTools for crb on EL8. The baseline names where minimal baselines come from.
When Packtrix loads the catalog, it checks every entry, and that every key file contains the key its fingerprint pins. make test-live also fetches the InRelease file of every repository, for every architecture, and verifies it with the pinned keys.
Vendor repositories will use the same fields as custom repositories, pre-filled:
# catalog/vendors/kubernetes.yaml name: kubernetes params: version: { required: true, pattern: '^1\.\d+$' } deb: url: "https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v{version}/deb/" suite: "/" rpm: url: "https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v{version}/rpm/" keys: [kubernetes-release] # → catalog/keys/, pinned by fingerprint Vendor URL layouts are irregular, and absorbing that is the catalog’s job. For example, Docker uses its centos path for Rocky and AlmaLinux, but its rhel path for RHEL.
data.components#Components:
distro.components selects parts of the distribution. It is the same field for every family:
Ubuntu Debian Rocky / Alma / RHEL / CentOS Stream Default main, universe main baseos, appstream Optional restricted, multiverse contrib, non-free, non-free-firmware crb, extras, highavailability The catalog maps these to vendor-specific names. For example, crb becomes powertools on EL8 and codeready-builder-… on RHEL. Ubuntu defaults to main plus universe because many common server packages, such as glusterfs-client on 24.04, live in universe.
data.inclusion-policy#Inclusion policy:
A repository is added to the catalog only if:
it is the official repository of the vendor or project, not a mirror, PPA or personal repository; it is signed, and its key fingerprint is published in the vendor’s own documentation; it is used widely enough to justify maintenance.
data.maintenance#Maintenance:
Repositories move and keys rotate. For example, Kubernetes moved from apt.kubernetes.io to pkgs.k8s.io in 2023, and the old repositories were later shut down. The catalog is maintained like this:
Nightly checks in CI: for every entry, fetch the index, verify its signature with the pinned key, and resolve a test package. Broken entries are found before users hit them. Separate release cycle: the catalog is versioned independently of the binary. packtrix catalog update fetches a newer signed catalog, and a snapshot is embedded in each binary so it works offline. Pinned in the lockfile: the catalog version is recorded, so updating the catalog never changes an existing lockfile silently. Organization catalogs (planned): --catalog adds your own entries next to the built-in ones.
data.where-the-data-comes-from#Where the data: Each catalog release ships a name index: which package names each vendor repository provides, for each distro and architecture. At plan time, Packtrix also reads the live index of each candidate repository, so packages that a vendor added after the catalog release are still found.

data:
Status: early development. This works today for Ubuntu and Debian targets, with distro and custom repositories. Planned: RPM, built-in vendor repositories (and repo:), discovery, and bundles.
This page defines the vocabulary used everywhere else in the docs.
data.baseline#Baseline:
A dependency closure is always relative to what the machine already has. The baseline sets that starting point:
Baseline Meaning Use it when minimal (default) A minimal installation of the distro, at its release versions, is assumed. What it already contains isn’t downloaded unless you list it. Machines are installed from the distro’s own media none Nothing is assumed. Everything down to the C library is included. The offline repository must also patch the base system, or machines start from container images, which have less than a minimal installation lock: The exact package set of a discovered host You want only what one specific host is missing (planned, see discovery)
data.bundle#Bundle:
A bundle is a single file (tar.zst, optionally split into parts) that carries a snapshot across the air gap. It can be:
full: everything needed to build the repositories from scratch; delta: only what changed since a previous lockfile. Bundles are signed and include their lockfile. On the offline side, import verifies a bundle and adds it as a new snapshot. A bundle is a plain tar archive, so it can be unpacked even without Packtrix.
data.dependency-resolution#Dependency resolut: For each target, Packtrix computes every package the machines need from the repositories’ own metadata: the listed packages and their dependencies, minus what the baseline already provides. It follows the rules apt and dnf apply. Its results are compared nightly with what the real apt picks, and installed with it. It needs no container runtime. See Architecture.
data.lockfile#Lockfile:
plan writes packtrix.lock, and sync carries it out exactly. Commit the lockfile next to the manifest. For every target and architecture it records:
every package: name, exact version, architecture, source repository, URL, SHA-256, size, and why it is needed; each upstream repository: the digest of the Release file that was verified, and the fingerprint of the key that signed it; the version of the built-in catalog, and the digest of the manifest. apiVersion: packtrix.io/v1alpha1 kind: Lock metadata: name: k8s-node-prereqs spec: catalog: 2026.10.1 manifest: sha256:7cd658be… targets: - architecture: amd64 distribution: Ubuntu noble format: apt name: ubuntu-24.04 packages: - architecture: amd64 name: libcurl4t64 repository: updates sha256: 0f3c… size: 344300 url: https://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/pool/main/c/curl/libcurl4t64_8.5.0-2ubuntu10.16_amd64.deb version: 8.5.0-2ubuntu10.16 why: - curl repositories: - components: - main - universe name: updates release: sha256:9a1e… signer: F6ECB3762474EDA9D21B7022871920D1991BC93C suite: noble-updates url: https://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ The manifest says what you want; the lockfile says exactly what you got. An update is a lockfile diff, and that diff is what a reviewer approves. Its lists are sorted and it holds no timestamp, so planning the same thing twice writes the same file. The manifest’s digest is taken after defaults, so comments and formatting don’t count; a lock planned from another version of the manifest is stale.
data.other-resolution-settings#Other resoluti: Recommended packages (APT Recommends, RPM weak dependencies) are off by default. Alternatives (a | b in APT): the first alternative is used by default. Excluded packages are ones the machines get some other way. They satisfy every dependency on them and are never downloaded; plan lists the packages that need them.
data.package#Package:
The packages list is written once and resolved for every target.
packages: - curl # same name everywhere - name: apache # a label for the entry, plus the real names per format deb: apache2 rpm: httpd - name: kubelet version: "1.34.*" # version constraint - name: software-properties-common except: [debian-13] # not available on that target - name: nginx repo: nginx-org # take it from this vendor, not from the distro A package you list is always included, even if a minimal installation of the distro already contains it. If a listed package can’t be found for a target, plan fails. It is never skipped silently.
data.repository#Repository:
A repository is where Packtrix looks for packages. It is not what Packtrix downloads: only the packages you list, plus their dependencies, are downloaded. Adding a repository with 10,000 packages costs nothing if you need two of them.
There are three kinds:
Kind Example How it is added Distro repositories Ubuntu archive, -updates and -security; Rocky BaseOS and AppStream Automatically, from distro Built-in vendor repositories Docker, Kubernetes, NVIDIA, EPEL Automatically, when a listed package needs one (see auto-detection) Custom repositories Your internal repository; a distro that isn’t built in By you: extraRepos on a known distro, or repos for a target defined from scratch The distro always wins. If a package exists in the distro, the distro’s build is used. A vendor build is used only when you ask for it with repo:.
data.snapshot#Snapshot:
Every sync builds a new, immutable snapshot of all repositories. A current pointer switches to it atomically, so clients never see a half-built repository. Earlier snapshots are kept for rollback (publish.keepSnapshots).
Package files are stored once, in a content-addressed pool shared by every snapshot and target. Keeping five snapshots doesn’t take five times the space.
data.target#Target:
A target is one kind of machine in your offline environment: a distribution, a release and one or more architectures. Packtrix builds one repository per target.
There are two ways to define a target:
targets: # A distro Packtrix knows: its official repositories, signing keys and format are built in. - distro: ubuntu-24.04 # A distro Packtrix doesn't know: list its repositories yourself. - name: oracle-9 repos: - { name: ol9-baseos, type: rpm, url: "https://yum.oracle.com/repo/OracleLinux/OL9/baseos/latest/x86_64/", gpgKey: keys/RPM-GPG-KEY-oracle } You never type an OS name, version or package format. Packtrix reads them from the repositories’ own metadata: the APT Release file states Origin, Version and Codename, and an RPM distribution’s BaseOS repository contains its release package.
Dependencies are resolved within one target only. A target must never mix releases. If Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 repositories were mixed, the resolver would pick the newer 24.04 builds for every machine, and they wouldn’t install on 22.04. Packtrix rejects a target whose repositories disagree on distribution, release or format.

data:
This guide builds offline APT repositories for Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12 machines, from start to finish: install Packtrix, create a signing key, write a manifest, plan, sync, serve the result, and install packages on a machine. It takes about ten minutes, and downloads about 40 MB: 30 MB of upstream indexes, and the packages.
What works today: Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04, Debian 12 and 13, on amd64 and arm64. Planned: RPM distributions, vendor repositories that Packtrix adds by itself (Docker, Kubernetes, …), and bundles to carry across the air gap. See the roadmap.
data.1-install-packtrix#1. Install Packtrix:
Download the archive for your platform from the releases, with checksums.txt, and check it. OS is linux or darwin, and ARCH is amd64 or arm64:
VERSION=0.1.0 OS=linux ARCH=amd64 URL=https://github.com/packtrix/packtrix/releases/download/v$VERSION curl -fsSLO $URL/packtrix_${VERSION}_${OS}_${ARCH}.tar.gz curl -fsSLO $URL/checksums.txt sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt packtrix_0.1.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz: OK tar -xzf packtrix_${VERSION}_${OS}_${ARCH}.tar.gz packtrix sudo install packtrix /usr/local/bin/ packtrix version On macOS, shasum -a 256 --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt checks the archive. The checksums are signed by the release workflow: Releasing shows how to check the signature and the build provenance.
With Go 1.26 or newer, go install github.com/packtrix/packtrix/cmd/packtrix@latest builds Packtrix instead, and make build writes bin/packtrix from a clone of the repository.
data.2-create-a-signing-key#2. Create a signi:
Packtrix signs the repositories it builds, and the machines trust them through your public key. In a new directory for the project, create a key for this purpose only:
mkdir my-servers && cd my-servers export GNUPGHOME=$(mktemp -d) # don't touch your personal keyring gpg --batch --passphrase '' --quick-gen-key 'Packtrix Repository Signing ' rsa3072 sign never gpg --armor --export-secret-keys 'Packtrix Repository Signing' > signing-key.asc chmod 600 signing-key.asc The export names the key, so it can’t take other keys along if GNUPGHOME isn’t set: the file must hold exactly one key. The key must be RSA of at least 3072 bits, or Ed25519, and must not be protected by a passphrase (support for passphrases is planned).
Keep signing-key.asc secret: whoever has it can sign packages your machines will trust. If the directory is a Git repository, add signing-key.asc to its .gitignore. In CI, put the key in a secret and reference it as env:PACKTRIX_SIGNING_KEY instead of a file.
data.3-write-a-manifest#3. Write a manifest:
packtrix init writes a starter manifest for the distros your machines run, and the packages they need:
packtrix init --target ubuntu-24.04 --target debian-12 --package curl,jq,nginx,rsync -f packtrix.yaml Wrote packtrix.yaml. Next: run packtrix plan. # yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/packtrix/packtrix/main/schemas/v1alpha1/offlinerepository.json # A Packtrix manifest: the machines you run, and the packages they need. # Every field: https://packtrix.github.io/docs/manifest/ apiVersion: packtrix.io/v1alpha1 kind: OfflineRepository metadata: name: my-servers spec: # The kinds of machines, one repository each. packtrix catalog list shows # the distros. For arm64 machines, add architectures: [amd64, arm64]. targets: - distro: ubuntu-24.04 - distro: debian-12 # What the machines need. Packtrix adds the dependencies. packages: - curl - jq - nginx - rsync # The machines already have a minimal installation of their distro. If they # are containers, which have less, Packtrix can include everything: # resolve: # baseline: none publish: # The OpenPGP private key that signs the repositories, as file:/path or # env:NAME. Keep it secret. signing: key: file:signing-key.asc The manifest is named after its directory; --name sets another name. The first line points editors to the manifest’s JSON Schema, so they complete fields and flag mistakes: see editor support.
targets names the distributions. packtrix catalog list shows the built-in ones, and packtrix catalog show ubuntu-24.04 their repositories and the keys Packtrix trusts for them. packages is one list for every target. A package can be limited to some targets, have a version constraint such as "1.34.*", or a different name per format: see the manifest reference. The baseline is what the machines already have. By default, minimal, Packtrix assumes a minimal installation of the distro, from its release media, and only downloads what that lacks. If the machines are containers, which have less, add resolve: { baseline: none }: everything, down to the C library, goes into the repository. Check the manifest, and see the repositories it uses:
packtrix validate packtrix.yaml is valid: 2 target(s), 4 package(s) packtrix render
data.4-plan#4. Plan:
plan reads the metadata of every repository, checks its signature against the pinned keys, and resolves the packages and their dependencies for each target. It downloads no package. The indexes it reads are cached (in ~/.cache/packtrix on Linux, or --cache-dir), so the next plan only fetches what changed upstream.
packtrix plan Reading ubuntu-24.04 (amd64): release, https://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ noble Reading ubuntu-24.04 (amd64): updates, https://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ noble-updates Reading ubuntu-24.04 (amd64): security, https://security.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ noble-security Reading debian-12 (amd64): release, https://deb.debian.org/debian/ bookworm … Wrote packtrix.lock ubuntu-24.04 (amd64): Ubuntu noble, 16 packages, 2.8 MiB REPOSITORY SUITE PACKAGES SIGNED BY release noble 70854 F6ECB3762474EDA9D21B7022871920D1991BC93C updates noble-updates 15230 F6ECB3762474EDA9D21B7022871920D1991BC93C security noble-security 11770 F6ECB3762474EDA9D21B7022871920D1991BC93C PACKAGE VERSION SIZE WHY curl 8.5.0-2ubuntu10.16 221.1 KiB listed jq 1.7.1-3ubuntu0.24.04.2 64.2 KiB listed nginx 1.24.0-2ubuntu7.18 512.3 KiB listed rsync 3.2.7-1ubuntu1.5 432.6 KiB listed libcurl4t64 8.5.0-2ubuntu10.16 336.3 KiB curl libjq1 1.7.1-3ubuntu0.24.04.2 138.6 KiB jq nginx-common 1.24.0-2ubuntu7.18 44.0 KiB nginx … libsasl2-modules-db 2.1.28+dfsg1-5ubuntu3.1 19.9 KiB curl → libcurl4t64 → libldap2 → libsasl2-2 debian-12 (amd64): Debian bookworm, 16 packages, 2.9 MiB … 2 target(s), 32 package files to download, 5.7 MiB For each target, plan shows the repositories it read, with the key that signed each, and the packages to download. WHY is the chain that brings a package in: libsasl2-modules-db is there because curl needs libcurl4t64, which needs libldap2, and so on. Packages the baseline already has aren’t listed.
The result goes to packtrix.lock: the exact version, URL and SHA-256 of every package, and the key that signed each repository. Commit the manifest and the lock: sync downloads exactly what the lock says, and an update is a diff of the lock that you can review.
If a package doesn’t exist, or a dependency can’t be satisfied, plan says which, with the chain of packages that needs it, and writes no lock.
data.5-sync#5. Sync:
sync carries out the lock: it downloads the packages, checks each one against the lock, and builds one signed repository per target. --base-url is the URL where the machines will reach the result.
packtrix sync --base-url http://repo.internal Downloaded debian-12 (amd64): 16 packages, 16 new, 2.9 MiB Downloaded ubuntu-24.04 (amd64): 16 packages, 16 new, 2.8 MiB TARGET SUITE ARCHITECTURES PACKAGES SIZE debian-12 bookworm amd64 16 2.9 MiB ubuntu-24.04 noble amd64 16 2.8 MiB Published repos/current (snapshot 2026-10-26T161035Z). Each machine needs two files: see repos/current/clients/README. Everything is in publish.path, ./repos by default:
repos/ ├── current -> snapshots/2026-10-26T161035Z what the machines use ├── snapshots/2026-10-26T161035Z/ │ ├── apt/ubuntu-24.04/ one signed repository per target │ ├── apt/debian-12/ │ ├── clients/ a source entry per target, and a README │ ├── keys/ your public key │ └── packtrix.lock └── pool/ every package file, once Each sync builds a new snapshot, then switches current to it in one step: machines never see a half-built repository, and a sync that fails leaves the published one as it was. A second sync downloads only what changed.
data.6-serve-the-repositories#6. Serve the re:
Serve repos/current at the base URL with any web server. With nginx:
server { listen 80; server_name repo.internal; root /srv/repos/current; } To try it out, python3 -m http.server 8080 --directory repos/current serves it on port 8080 (then use --base-url http://:8080).
In a container, mount repos and serve its current from inside, so that each sync is served as soon as it’s published:
docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -v "$PWD/repos:/repos:ro" python:3.13-alpine \ python -m http.server 8080 --directory /repos/current A mount of repos/current itself stays on the snapshot it pointed to when the container started; Docker Desktop can even resolve it to an older one.
Plain HTTP is fine: the machines check every file against your signature, not against the transport. See security.
Across the air gap: bundles (packtrix export and import) are planned. Until then, copy the published directory with any tool, and serve it on the other side:
tar -C repos/current -czf my-servers.tar.gz . # offline side mkdir -p /srv/repos/current && tar -C /srv/repos/current -xzf my-servers.tar.gz
data.7-configure-the-machines#7. Configure th:
Each machine needs two files from repos/current: its target’s source entry, clients/.sources, and the public key, keys/packtrix-repo.gpg. clients/README lists them, with the fingerprint of the key. Copy them to the machine the way you deploy other configuration (scp, Ansible, an image build), and put them in place:
# on an Ubuntu 24.04 machine sudo install -D -m 644 packtrix-repo.gpg /etc/apt/keyrings/packtrix-repo.gpg sudo install -m 644 ubuntu-24.04.sources /etc/apt/sources.list.d/packtrix.sources # /etc/apt/sources.list.d/packtrix.sources Types: deb URIs: http://repo.internal/apt/ubuntu-24.04/ Suites: noble Components: main Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/packtrix-repo.gpg A machine without Internet access should have no other source, or apt-get update reports errors for them. Move the distro’s own entries aside: /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ubuntu.sources on Ubuntu 24.04, /etc/apt/sources.list on Ubuntu 22.04, /etc/apt/sources.list.d/debian.sources on Debian. Then:
sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install curl jq nginx rsync apt installs from your repository like from any other: the listed packages, and the dependencies that the machine doesn’t have yet.
data.8-update#8. Update:
Upstream publishes fixes all the time. To bring them in, plan again: the lock changes, and its diff shows what moved.
packtrix plan git diff packtrix.lock # review the new versions packtrix sync --base-url http://repo.internal sync publishes a new snapshot, and keeps the previous ones next to it (publish.keepSnapshots, 3 by default); they share the package files, so they take little space. The machines pick up the changes with apt-get update and apt-get upgrade. To add a package, add it to the manifest, then plan and sync.
data.next#Next: Concepts: targets, the baseline, the lock and snapshots, in more depth. Manifest reference: every field, such as components, mirrors, extra repositories, and credentials. Workflow: every command, and how updates are reviewed. Security: what Packtrix verifies, and what your machines trust.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Message What to do unknown distro "ubuntu-24.4"; did you mean "ubuntu-24.04"? Use a name from packtrix catalog list. no package foo in the target's repositories The package doesn’t exist in that distro, or is in a component the target doesn’t use, such as restricted. Add the component with distro: { name: …, components: [main, universe, restricted] }, or limit the package to other targets with only:. … needs libfoo (>= 2), which no package provides A dependency can’t be satisfied from the target’s repositories. The chain shows which package needs it. the server's certificate isn't trusted …; pass its certificate with --ca-file A proxy or mirror uses a private certificate authority: pass its certificate with --ca-file to plan and sync. the lock was planned from another version of the manifest; run packtrix plan The manifest changed since the last plan. Plan again. the repository changed since the lock was planned, …; run packtrix plan sync runs on another machine than plan, or the cache was cleared, and upstream has moved on since. Plan again, or keep the cache (--cache-dir) between plan and sync. publish.signing.key is required to sign the repositories Add publish.signing.key to the manifest. another sync is writing repos Another sync uses the same publish.path. Wait for it.
data.what-you-need#What you need: A Linux or macOS machine with Internet access: the connected side. It reaches the official archives (archive.ubuntu.com, security.ubuntu.com, deb.debian.org, security.debian.org) directly, or through the proxy in HTTPS_PROXY. GnuPG, once, to create the key that signs your repositories. On the offline side, any web server, to serve the repositories to the machines.

data:
Status: packtrix.io/v1alpha1, an alpha API. Fields and defaults may still change in later releases; the release notes say what changed.
Packtrix reads packtrix.yaml from the current directory by default. Use -f to choose another file.
data.auth-object#Auth object:
Used in distro.auth and in repository objects:
Field Description username, password Basic authentication. Set both. password is a secret reference. token Bearer token, as a secret reference. Can’t be combined with password. clientCert, clientKey Paths to a TLS client certificate and its key. Set both. entitlement Directory holding RHEL subscription certificates, usually /etc/pki/entitlement A secret reference is env:NAME (read an environment variable) or file:/path (read a file). Secrets themselves never appear in the manifest.
data.distro-as-an-object#distro as an object:
Use the object form only to change a distro’s defaults:
distro: name: rocky-9 components: [baseos, appstream, crb] mirror: https://nexus.internal/repository/ auth: { … } Field Default Description name — Built-in distro name components per distro Parts of the distro to include. The same field works for every distro family. See components. mirror official servers Fetch through a mirror or proxy (Nexus, Artifactory, a local mirror) instead of the official servers. Each repository keeps its path under the mirror, and its keys. With https://nexus.internal/repository/, Ubuntu’s https://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ becomes https://nexus.internal/repository/ubuntu/, its arm64 archive …/ubuntu-ports/, and Debian’s security archive …/debian-security/. packtrix render shows the resulting URLs. auth — Credentials for distros that need them, e.g. RHEL subscription certificates
data.editor-support#Editor support:
A JSON Schema of the manifest, schemas/v1alpha1/offlinerepository.json, lets editors complete fields and values, show what each field does and its default, and mark mistakes as you type. Editors that use the YAML language server, such as VS Code with Red Hat’s YAML extension, or Neovim, find it through a comment in the manifest:
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/packtrix/packtrix/main/schemas/v1alpha1/offlinerepository.json Other editors can map the schema to packtrix.yaml in their settings. The schema checks each field like packtrix validate, but not the rules across fields, such as unique target names or only naming an existing target: packtrix validate still has the last word. It is generated from the API types, with make update-schema.
data.examples#Examples: examples/k8s-node-prereqs.yaml: Kubernetes node prerequisites for Ubuntu 24.04, Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian 12 examples/mixed-fleet.yaml: Ubuntu, Rocky and RHEL with Docker, Kubernetes and NVIDIA packages examples/custom-repos.yaml: an internal repository and a distro defined from scratch
data.full-structure#Full structure: apiVersion: packtrix.io/v1alpha1 kind: OfflineRepository metadata: name: datacenter spec: targets: # which machines (required) - name: ubuntu-gpu # default: the distro name distro: ubuntu-24.04 # built-in distro … architectures: [amd64, arm64] # default: [amd64] extraRepos: [] # … plus your own repositories - name: oracle-9 repos: [] # … or a distro defined from scratch packages: [] # what the machines need (required) autoRepos: # automatic vendor repositories enabled: true deny: [] resolve: # how dependencies are resolved baseline: minimal recommends: false alternatives: first exclude: [] updates: # how updates are picked up check: "" accept: all minAge: 0s publish: approval publish: # where and how repositories are written path: ./repos signing: {} keepSnapshots: 3 export: # how bundles are written format: tar.zst splitSize: ""
data.minimal-manifest#Minimal manifest: apiVersion: packtrix.io/v1alpha1 kind: OfflineRepository metadata: name: datacenter spec: targets: - distro: ubuntu-24.04 - distro: rocky-9 packages: [curl, jq, nfs-common] Everything else has a default.
data.repository-object#Repository object:
Used in extraRepos and repos:
Field Required Description name yes Unique name type yes apt or rpm url yes Base URL. {arch} is replaced with the native architecture name. suite apt only e.g. stable, noble, or / for a flat repository components apt only e.g. [main]. Not used for flat repositories. gpgKey yes Path to the repository’s public signing key auth no Credentials (basic auth, bearer token, client certificate), as references to environment variables or files, never as literal values extraRepos: - name: internal-tools type: apt url: https://pkgs.internal/apt suite: stable components: [main] gpgKey: keys/internal.gpg
data.specautorepos#spec.autoRepos: Field Default Description enabled true Add built-in vendor repositories automatically when a package needs one. See auto-detection. deny [] Repositories that must never be added automatically, as glob patterns, e.g. [epel-*]
data.specexport#spec.export: Field Default Description format tar.zst Bundle format splitSize (none) Split bundles into parts of this size, e.g. 4GiB for FAT32 media or transfer-system limits
data.specpackages#spec.packages:
A list of packages, written once for all targets. An entry is either a string (the package name) or an object:
Field Description name Package name. When deb/rpm are set, it is only a label. version Version constraint (see below). Also selects the repository for vendors that publish one repository per version, such as Kubernetes. deb / rpm The real package name for that format, when it differs only Include this package only for these targets. Values are target names, or deb/rpm for a whole format. except Include it for every target except these. Cannot be combined with only. repo Take the package from this built-in vendor repository instead of the distro, e.g. nginx-org
data.specpublish#spec.publish: Field Default Description path ./repos Output directory. A relative path starts from the manifest’s directory. Machines are served from /current. signing.key — Reference to the private signing key, e.g. env:PACKTRIX_SIGNING_KEY or file:/path. Required to publish APT repositories. keepSnapshots 3 Number of earlier snapshots kept next to the current one, for rollback. Their package files are hard links into the pool, so they take little space.
data.specresolve#spec.resolve: Field Default Description baseline minimal minimal, none, or lock:. See baseline. recommends false Include APT Recommends and RPM weak dependencies alternatives first For APT a | b dependencies: first or all exclude [] Packages that the machines get some other way, such as a driver installed by hand. They satisfy every dependency on them, at any version, and are never downloaded; plan lists the packages that need them. A package that is listed is still downloaded.
data.spectargets#spec.targets:
A list of targets. A target is either a short form - distro: or an object:
Field Type Default Description name string value of distro Unique name. Used in only/except and in output paths. distro string or object — A built-in distro (see catalog). Exactly one of distro or repos is required. architectures list [amd64] Normalized names: amd64, arm64. Rendered as x86_64/aarch64 for RPM. extraRepos list of repository [] Your repositories added on top of the distro, e.g. an internal repository. repos list of repository — The complete repository list for a distro Packtrix doesn’t know. Vendor repositories aren’t detected automatically for these targets.
data.specupdates#spec.updates: Field Default Description check (empty: manual) Cron expression for update checks when Packtrix runs as a scheduled job accept all all, security (security updates only), or none (keep the lockfile pinned) minAge 0s Wait this long after a new version is published before taking it, e.g. 72h publish approval auto: publish after validation. approval: stop after plan until the lockfile change is approved.
data.validation-rules#Validation rules:
packtrix validate and packtrix plan reject a manifest when:
it contains an unknown or duplicated field. A typo such as architecture: instead of architectures: is an error, never silently ignored; a target has both distro and repos, or neither; two targets have the same name; only or except names an unknown target; an entry has both only and except; a target’s repositories disagree on distribution, release or format; a listed package isn’t available for a target it applies to; a package from a versioned vendor repository (e.g. Kubernetes) has no version; a package matches several unrelated vendor repositories and has no repo. Every error names the target, the package and what to change.
data.version-constraints#Version constraints:
Constraint Matches (none) Newest available "1.34.1" Upstream version 1.34.1, any packaging revision "1.34.*" Any 1.34.x "1.34.1-1.1" That exact package version Versions are compared with each format’s native rules (dpkg ordering for deb; rpm ordering, including epochs, for rpm).
Always quote versions. Unquoted, YAML reads 1.30 as the number 1.3. Packtrix rejects unquoted numeric versions rather than guess.

data.design-principles#Design principles: One manifest for APT and RPM. The package list is written once. Differences between formats are per-package exceptions, not separate sections. Built-in resolution, checked against apt and dnf. Packtrix resolves dependencies itself, from the repositories’ metadata, following the rules apt and dnf apply. It needs no container runtime, and its results are checked against the real tools. Complete or nothing. If a package or one of its dependencies can’t be resolved for a target, plan fails and names the package, the target and the reason. A partial repository is never published. Everything that crosses the air gap is recorded. The lockfile lists every package, version, checksum and source. Standard output. Plain APT and RPM repositories. Machines need no agent, plugin or special client. Light offline side. The connected side resolves and downloads. The offline side only verifies, stores and serves, using a single binary or any web server.
data.related-tools#Related tools: Tool Focus How Packtrix differs aptly APT repository management: mirrors with dependency filtering, snapshots, publishing Packtrix covers APT and RPM from one manifest Pulp / Katello / Red Hat Satellite Content management platforms for RPM and Debian content Packtrix is a single CLI with no server stack, focused on producing offline repositories Nexus / Artifactory Hosting and proxying many package formats Proxies cache what clients request. Packtrix computes the complete set before the transfer. Zarf / Hauler Air-gap delivery of Kubernetes content: images, charts, files They don’t resolve OS package dependencies. The two complement each other.
data.the-problem#The problem:
Many Linux machines run without internet access: defense and public-sector networks, banks, critical infrastructure, factories, ships, labs. They still need packages, both to install software and to receive security fixes.
The usual options are all costly:
Approach Cost Mirror entire distributions Hundreds of GB per release and architecture, most of which is never used. In regulated networks every file that crosses the air gap must be scanned and approved, so size matters. Scripts per distro (apt-get download, dnf download --resolve) One script per distro and release. They miss dependencies that happen to be installed on the preparing machine, don’t sign anything, and don’t handle updates. Repository platforms (Pulp/Katello, Nexus, Artifactory, …) Built for connected networks, or a server stack to deploy and operate just to produce a few repositories. Mixed fleets double the work: Ubuntu and RHEL-family machines need two toolchains, two sets of scripts and two sets of keys.
data.use-cases#Use cases: Air-gapped Kubernetes nodes. Node prerequisites (conntrack, socat, ipvsadm, storage clients), the container runtime and kubelet/kubeadm, for both Ubuntu and RHEL-family nodes, from one manifest. Regulated and sovereign networks. An approved package set where every change is a reviewed diff. The lockfile serves as the audit trail of what entered the network. Offline security patching. A scheduled job picks up security updates only and ships them as a small delta bundle. Edge and remote sites. Small repositories and small updates for sites with slow or intermittent links. Mixed fleets and migrations. Moving from Ubuntu 22.04 to 24.04, or from CentOS to Rocky, means adding a target. The package list stays the same. Reproducible image builds. Packer or CI image builds install from a pinned snapshot instead of from whatever upstream serves that day. Rebuilding a host (planned). Inspect an existing server and generate the manifest that reproduces its packages.
data.what-packtrix-does#What Packtrix does:
Input: the distros your machines run, and the packages they need.
Output: for every distro, a signed repository containing those packages and all their dependencies, ready to carry across the air gap and serve with any web server.
spec: targets: - distro: ubuntu-24.04 - distro: rocky-9 packages: [curl, jq, docker-ce, nfs-common]
data.what-packtrix-is-not#What Packtrix is no: Not this Use instead A full mirror of a distribution apt-mirror, debmirror, reposync A caching proxy for connected networks Nexus, Artifactory, a pull-through cache A tool to build your own .deb/.rpm packages nFPM, fpm, distro build tooling A transport for container images or Helm charts Zarf, Hauler, registry mirroring Configuration management Ansible, Salt, Puppet Packtrix can work alongside these tools. A Packtrix bundle can travel next to container images in the same air-gap transfer.
data.who-it-is-for#Who it is for: Platform and infrastructure teams who run Linux machines in offline or air-gapped environments. Security teams who must approve what enters those environments. Teams building offline installers, such as Kubernetes distributions, appliances or on-premises products, who need their OS-level prerequisites bundled.

data: Packtrix sits on the supply chain of the machines it serves, so every release can be verified: who built it, from which commit, and that nothing changed since.
data.cutting-a-release#Cutting a release:
Check that main is ready:
CI is green, including the nightly e2e and compare workflows; the release’s milestone has no open issues; the docs describe what the release does, and the install commands in README.md and docs/getting-started.md name its version. Try the release locally. make release-snapshot builds everything into dist/, without signing or publishing.
Tag the commit on main, and push the tag:
git switch main && git pull git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "v0.1.0" git push origin v0.1.0 A tag with a suffix, such as v0.2.0-rc.1, makes a pre-release.
Watch the release workflow. When it’s done, verify the release as below, then edit the release notes on GitHub if needed.
If the workflow fails, fix the cause on main. Then delete the tag, and the GitHub release if the workflow created one, and tag again.
data.verifying-a-release#Verifying a release:
Download the archive for your platform, with checksums.txt and its signature:
gh release download v0.1.0 --repo packtrix/packtrix \ --pattern 'packtrix_*_linux_amd64.tar.gz' --pattern 'checksums.txt*' 1. The signature of the checksums, with cosign. It proves that the release workflow of packtrix/packtrix signed this checksums.txt, when building this tag:
cosign verify-blob checksums.txt \ --bundle checksums.txt.sigstore.json \ --certificate-identity https://github.com/packtrix/packtrix/.github/workflows/release.yaml@refs/tags/v0.1.0 \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com Verified OK 2. The archive against the checksums:
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt packtrix_0.1.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz: OK 3. The build provenance, with the GitHub CLI, version 2.49 or newer: older versions, such as the one in Ubuntu 24.04’s archive, have no attestation command. It shows the repository, workflow and commit that built the archive:
gh attestation verify packtrix_0.1.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz --repo packtrix/packtrix Then install the binary, and check its version:
tar -xzf packtrix_0.1.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz packtrix sudo install packtrix /usr/local/bin/ packtrix version
data.what-a-release-contains#What a release c:
The release workflow runs GoReleaser for each v* tag, and publishes a GitHub release with:
File What it is packtrix___.tar.gz The static binary for linux and darwin, amd64 and arm64, with LICENSE and README.md ….tar.gz.sbom.json The SBOM of each archive, in SPDX, written by syft checksums.txt The SHA-256 of every archive and SBOM checksums.txt.sigstore.json A keyless Sigstore signature of checksums.txt, made with the identity of the release workflow The workflow also attests the build provenance of every file in checksums.txt, with GitHub’s artifact attestations. Release notes list the pull requests merged since the previous release, not since its release candidates, grouped by the type of their title: features, fixes, documentation, and the rest.

data: Status: proposal. Phases describe priorities, not dates.
data.later#Later: Kubernetes: a CronJob example first; an operator only if real users need it Bundles as OCI artifacts, to travel through registries next to container images A libsolv-based resolver, if the built-in closure meets cases it can’t handle Locally built packages added to the output (createrepo_c) Organization catalogs
data.open-questions#Open questions: # Question Current leaning 1 What does exclude mean when an excluded package is a dependency of a listed one? Decided: it is provided some other way, like the baseline. It satisfies the dependency, isn’t downloaded, and plan reports it 2 Default for APT alternatives (a | b) first, with all available 3 Per-target version pins, e.g. different kubelet versions per target Not in v1alpha1; use separate manifests if needed 4 Per-target update policy Not in v1alpha1 5 Multi-arch APT (foreign architectures such as i386) Out of scope for v1alpha1 6 EL8 modular content Carry modules.yaml through; needs testing with real AppStream content 7 API group domain for apiVersion Decided: packtrix.io 8 Bundle format Plain tar.zst first, OCI artifact later
data.phase-0-design#Phase 0: Design: Problem statement, goals and non-goals Manifest draft (packtrix.io/v1alpha1) Architecture and trust model Feedback from real air-gapped environments Decide the open questions that block Phase 1
data.phase-1-apt-end-to-end-v010-done#Phase 1:
Goal: one manifest produces working, signed APT repositories on a local disk, for Ubuntu and Debian. Getting started shows what works.
Manifest parsing, defaults, validation JSON Schema of the manifest, for editors Catalog: ubuntu-22.04, ubuntu-24.04, debian-12, debian-13, on amd64 and arm64 Dependency resolution in Go for APT Resolution checked nightly against apt Download, upstream signature verification, content-addressed pool APT metadata subsetting and signing packtrix.lock Generated client files (clients/) and keys (keys/) Commands: init, validate, render, plan, sync, catalog Integration tests: install from the generated repositories in clean containers of each distro Release pipeline: archives, SBOMs, signed checksums and build provenance (releasing) The v0.1.0 release RPM targets are valid in a manifest, but plan reports them as not supported yet.

data:
Status: early development. The APT parts work as described. RPM, bundles, and signed catalog releases are planned.
Packtrix sits on the supply chain of every machine it serves. This page describes how trust flows from upstream vendors to those machines, and what Packtrix asserts at each step.
data.built-in-catalog-trust#Built-in catalog:
Shipping repository definitions and keys makes the built-in catalog a trust anchor. Rules:
Only official vendor repositories are included, with keys whose fingerprints match the vendor’s own documentation. Every catalog change that adds or changes a key is reviewed against that documentation. Catalog releases are versioned, and (planned) signed. The version used is recorded in the lockfile, so a catalog update never silently changes an existing lockfile. packtrix catalog show and packtrix render print exactly which URLs and key fingerprints will be used. (Planned, with vendor repositories) autoRepos.deny lets an organization forbid repositories it doesn’t accept, e.g. EPEL.
data.bundles#Bundles:
(Planned.)
Every bundle has a signed manifest with the SHA-256 of each file. import refuses bundles with a bad signature, a missing file or a hash mismatch, and refuses deltas whose base snapshot doesn’t match the offline side.
data.fetching-from-upstream#Fetching from ups: APT security doesn’t depend on transport, because the signatures above protect the content. Plain HTTP upstreams such as the Ubuntu archive are fine. For networks that intercept TLS or only reach the internet through a proxy, Packtrix uses the proxy of HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY, and trusts the system’s certificate authorities, those of SSL_CERT_FILE, and those of --ca-file. When a certificate isn’t trusted, the error names the host and suggests --ca-file. Authenticated upstreams (RHEL subscription certificates, tokens, basic auth, TLS client certificates) are configured with auth, as references to environment variables or files, never as literal values in the manifest. Packtrix never prints credentials: messages show URLs without their password, and a redirect to another host doesn’t carry the credentials along.
data.principles#Principles: Verify everything at the gate. No package enters the pool unless it traces back to an upstream signature made by a pinned key. Never trust a key fetched at runtime. Keys come from the built-in catalog or your manifest and are pinned by fingerprint. Make trust changes visible. A new repository or a new signing key appears in plan and in the lockfile diff, so a reviewer sees it before it takes effect. A checksum is not authenticity. A matching SHA-256 proves a file is the one the index describes. Only the signature on that index proves the index came from the vendor.
data.reporting-a-vulnerability#Reporting a vu: Please report vulnerabilities privately, through GitHub: SECURITY.md says how, and what to expect.
data.serving-on-the-offline-side#Serving on t: Default: plain HTTP plus GPG. This is the standard Debian model. Content integrity and authenticity come from the signatures, not from TLS. HTTPS is optional with a certificate you provide. Air-gapped networks can’t use public ACME CAs, so the certificate usually comes from an internal CA. Bootstrap: machines need the repository key (and, for HTTPS, the internal CA certificate) before they can use the repository. The generated clients/ and keys/ directories contain everything to copy onto a machine. Distributing those files belongs to your provisioning process (image build, cloud-init, configuration management). For production, serving /srv/repos/current with nginx, Apache or Caddy is recommended. packtrix serve (planned) is meant for small setups and testing.
data.signing-the-published-repositories#Signi:
This is where APT and RPM differ, and it matters for what your machines trust:
Format What happens What machines trust APT Packtrix publishes a subset of the upstream suite, so the upstream InRelease signature no longer matches. Packtrix writes a new InRelease and signs it with your key. Your key. Machines trust Packtrix’s output, which Packtrix built only from upstream-verified content. RPM Package signatures are embedded in the files and survive unchanged. Packtrix also signs repomd.xml with your key. The vendor’s keys, end to end, with gpgcheck=1. Your key is used only for the metadata (repo_gpgcheck=1). The client files Packtrix generates set this up correctly for each format.
data.verifying-upstream-content#Verifying ups:
Format How the trust chain works upstream What Packtrix verifies APT The signed InRelease file lists hashes of the Packages indexes, which list hashes of each .deb. Individual .deb files are not signed. The InRelease signature against the pinned key, then each index hash, then each .deb hash RPM Each .rpm carries an embedded GPG signature. Most distributions don’t sign repomd.xml. Each package’s signature against the pinned key, then each file hash against the metadata A signature only counts if it was made by a pinned key that is still valid: Packtrix, like apt, rejects signatures by keys that have since expired or been revoked, SHA-1 signatures, and DSA and ElGamal keys. An InRelease file must contain nothing outside its signed part. Like apt, Packtrix also rejects a Release file whose Valid-Until has passed, or that is for another suite than the one asked for, so a server or a mirror on the way can’t serve outdated metadata, or another suite’s. Only the SHA-256 hashes of a Release file count.
If any check fails, sync stops and nothing is published.
data.your-signing-key#Your signing key: Referenced from the manifest (publish.signing.key), never embedded in it: env:VAR or file:/path. Support for key management services is planned. Signing is done in-process (Go OpenPGP), with no gpg binary or agent required. It must be an OpenPGP version 4 key, RSA of at least 3072 bits or Ed25519, valid, and not protected by a passphrase (passphrases are planned). Packtrix signs with SHA-512. RHEL 9 rejects SHA-1 signatures, current apt warns about weak keys, and the gpgv that apt runs can’t verify version 6 keys. Rotation: machines pin your key with Signed-By/gpgkey. To rotate, publish signatures from both the old and new keys during an overlap period, update the client files, then retire the old key. Expiry: Packtrix doesn’t set Valid-Until on the Release files it publishes. An offline repository that “expires” after a week would break machines that can’t fetch a new one. Upstream Valid-Until values are ignored for content that has already been verified at sync time.

data:
Status: partly implemented. init, validate, render, plan, sync and catalog list | show work for Ubuntu and Debian. The rest is marked planned: a proposal that may change. To try what works, follow Getting started.
Packtrix runs in two places:
CONNECTED SIDE OFFLINE SIDE (build machine or CI, has internet) (no internet access) ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ packtrix.yaml + packtrix.lock (git) │ │ packtrix import │ │ packtrix plan │ bundle │ verify signature │ │ packtrix sync │ ────────► │ add snapshot, switch │ │ packtrix export │ USB, │ packtrix serve (or nginx) │ │ │ diode, … │ │ └──────────────────────────────────────┘ └──────────────────────────────┘ Connected side: the packtrix binary, with access to the upstream repositories. This is where the manifest, the lockfile and the downloads live. Offline side: only the packtrix binary to import bundles. Any web server can serve the result.
data.approval-through-git#Approval through Gi:
When updates.publish is approval, the lockfile in Git is the approval gate:
A scheduled CI job runs packtrix plan. Once packtrix check exists, it runs that first, and plans only if something changed. The job opens a pull request with the new packtrix.lock. A reviewer reads the diff: what changes, which repositories and keys are new. Merging the pull request triggers packtrix sync, and packtrix export once it exists. No server or operator is needed. This is the same model as dependency-update bots.
data.commands#Commands: Command Side What it does packtrix init connected Write a starter manifest, e.g. --target ubuntu-24.04 --target debian-12 --package curl. It prints it, or writes it with -f, never over an existing file. packtrix validate both Check the manifest without network access packtrix render connected Print the fully expanded manifest: every built-in name replaced by its URLs, components and key fingerprints packtrix plan connected Resolve dependencies, write packtrix.lock, and print each target’s packages, why each is needed, and how much will be downloaded. -o json for scripts, --ca-file for a private certificate authority, --lock to write the lock elsewhere, --cache-dir for the cache of upstream indexes. Nothing is written unless every target is planned. packtrix sync connected Carry out the lockfile: download, verify, build a snapshot, publish it. --base-url is where the published directory is served, for the client files. With --verify-install (planned), first test-install it in containers. packtrix check (planned) connected A cheap check of whether any upstream repository changed. Exit code 0 = no change, 2 = changes, 1 = error. packtrix export (planned) connected Write a bundle: full, or --since for a delta packtrix import (planned) offline Verify a bundle and add it as a new snapshot packtrix serve (planned) offline Serve the repositories over HTTP, for small setups and testing packtrix rollback (planned) both Point current back at an earlier snapshot packtrix catalog list | show connected Inspect the built-in catalog. catalog update, to refresh it, is planned. packtrix discover (planned) connected Inspect an existing host over SSH and write a manifest for it
data.configuring-the-machines#Configuring the:
sync also writes ready-made client configuration under clients/, one file per target, plus the public keys under keys/:
/srv/repos/current/ ├── apt/ ubuntu-24.04/… debian-12/… one repository per target ├── rpm/ rocky-9/… planned ├── keys/ packtrix-repo.asc, packtrix-repo.gpg └── clients/ ubuntu-24.04.sources, rocky-9.repo (planned), README On each machine, copy two files: its client file and the repository key. clients/README lists them for each target.
clients/ubuntu-24.04.sources -> /etc/apt/sources.list.d/packtrix.sources keys/packtrix-repo.gpg -> /etc/apt/keyrings/packtrix-repo.gpg # /etc/apt/sources.list.d/packtrix.sources (Ubuntu 24.04) Types: deb URIs: http://repo.internal/apt/ubuntu-24.04/ Suites: noble Components: main Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/packtrix-repo.gpg URIs comes from sync --base-url, the URL where the published directory is served. Without it, the files use http://packtrix-repository.invalid, which apt refuses, so a missing URL can’t go unnoticed. A machine without internet access should have no other source, so move the distro’s own entries, such as /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ubuntu.sources, aside.
All packages for a target, from the distro and from vendors, are merged into one repository. Each machine therefore needs a single source entry.
data.day-1-build-and-ship#Day 1: build and sh:
# connected side packtrix init --target ubuntu-24.04 --target debian-12 > packtrix.yaml vi packtrix.yaml # list the packages packtrix plan # resolve; review what will be downloaded packtrix sync --base-url http://repo.internal # download, verify, build signed repositories packtrix export -o bundle-2026-10-22.tar.zst # planned # carry the bundle across the air gap # offline side packtrix import bundle-2026-10-22.tar.zst --to /srv/repos # planned packtrix serve /srv/repos # planned; or point any web server at /srv/repos/current Until export and import exist, copy the published directory across with any tool, as Getting started shows.
plan shows each target, the repositories it read with the key that signed each, and the packages to download with the reason each is needed:
ubuntu-24.04 (amd64): Ubuntu noble, 16 packages, 2.8 MiB REPOSITORY SUITE PACKAGES SIGNED BY release noble 70854 F6ECB3762474EDA9D21B7022871920D1991BC93C updates noble-updates 15230 F6ECB3762474EDA9D21B7022871920D1991BC93C security noble-security 11770 F6ECB3762474EDA9D21B7022871920D1991BC93C PACKAGE VERSION SIZE WHY curl 8.5.0-2ubuntu10.16 221.1 KiB listed libcurl4t64 8.5.0-2ubuntu10.16 336.3 KiB curl libldap2 2.6.10+dfsg-0ubuntu0.24.04.1 193.0 KiB curl → libcurl4t64 … Once vendor repositories are added automatically (planned), they appear in the repository table, with the package that needed each.
data.day-2-updates#Day 2: updates:
Today, packtrix plan writes the new lock and git diff packtrix.lock shows what changed. The commands marked planned below make it shorter:
packtrix check # planned; exit 2: something changed upstream packtrix plan # new lockfile; printing it as a diff is planned ubuntu-24.04 ~ openssl 3.0.13-0ubuntu3.4 → 3.0.13-0ubuntu3.5 [security] + libfoo1 1.2-1 new dependency of nginx - libbar0 0.9-2 no longer required git commit packtrix.lock # open a pull request; a reviewer approves the diff packtrix sync packtrix export --since -o delta-2026-10-29.tar.zst # planned # offline side: import the delta; the previous snapshot stays available for rollback packtrix import delta-2026-10-29.tar.zst --to /srv/repos # planned
data.deployment-setups#Deployment setups: Setup Where Packtrix runs How content crosses Fully air-gapped Connected build machine or CI Bundle on approved media or through a data diode DMZ / semi-connected A host in the DMZ Internal machines read directly from its web server GitOps CI pipeline Bundles published as CI artifacts, then moved by your transfer process Kubernetes (later) A CronJob running the same CLI Same as above
